blocks.body:
# SeamScript: Pitch Sequencing Research and Product Design

Research current through August 30, 2026.

## Technical summary

Build SeamScript as a controlled language for pitch-sequence questions.

The first release joins four tasks. It finds sequences, builds fair comparisons, estimates chances, and explains uncertainty.

A study can use approved remote data, models, and algorithms. It does not train an untested replacement.

The strongest product claim is access. A coach can write a precise study without Python or SQL.

The safest analysis claim is predictive. SeamScript must not call an observed difference a causal effect.

The language fits the challenge well. It shows new syntax, a real interpreter, and a useful demonstration. [Challenge details](https://syntax-summit.devpost.com/)

## Target users and product order

### 1. Pregame game-plan coordinator

This user prepares pitcher plans for an opponent or series. This is the best first target.

The workflow has a clear decision and allows human review. Public Statcast can support the demonstration.

Team data can add intended locations, call sources, scouting tags, and current pitcher availability.

[MLB game-plan role](https://www.mlb.com/news/rockies-add-data-and-game-plan-coordinator) [Catcher preparation](https://www.mlb.com/news/featured/catching-up-with-tim-cossins)

### 2. Catching coordinator or catcher scout

This user reviews pitch-selection decisions. The system must separate a call from pitch execution and framing.

Public Statcast does not identify who called a pitch. Pitchers can also call pitches with PitchCom.

A catcher-quality claim needs private call-source and intended-location data. Without it, show observed sequence quality only.

[PitchCom rules](https://www.mlb.com/news/mlb-pitchers-pitchcom-transmitters-2023-update)

### 3. In-game pitching coach or manager

This user needs three ranked options during a mound visit or inning break.

MLB limits mound visits to 30 seconds. The answer must use preloaded data and return within one second.

Call each result a `recommended option`. Do not call it an `optimal pitch`.

This workflow follows the pregame release. It has higher time pressure and more hidden context.

[MLB mound visits](https://www.mlb.com/glossary/rules/mound-visit) [2026 dugout pitch calls](https://www.mlb.com/news/rockies-call-pitches-from-dugout-2026-spring-training)

## Key findings

### 1. Sequence structure is real, but sequence names alone explain little.

A 2026 study found stable pitch motifs in 12.4 million records. Those motifs did not clearly explain ERA, wins, hits, or outs. [Motif study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.11904)

### 2. Physical differences carry useful sequence information.

Earlier work linked lower predictability in speed and movement with higher strikeout rates. It omitted count, inning, and detailed off-speed quality. [Predictability study](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.3233/JSA-170103)

### 3. Context must be part of every comparison.

Pitch choice depends on count, batter, game state, and pitcher skill. Public data also lacks the catcher’s intended target. [Propensity-score study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03492)

### 4. Recent models support short prediction tasks. They do not prove optimal strategy.

A 2026 Transformer separated swing-outs from balls in play with 0.811 ROC AUC. The paper warned that season gains can be high. [Counterfactual study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.17345)

### 5. Large world models add cost before they add clear value.

A 2026 model reported 0.722 F1. Its RNN baseline reported 0.720 F1 for the same binary task. [World-model study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.07030)

That paper also gives conflicting next-pitch accuracy values. Its abstract states 64 percent. Its results section states 84 percent.

### 6. Long simulations increase error.

The world-model study found fast error growth across longer sequences. It also found bias toward common fastballs.

### 7. Player-pair models lack enough public data.

The motif study found about 23 shared pitches for an average pitcher-batter pair. Use partial pooling, not isolated pair models.

## How to read the model scores

The study used a 2025 time test. It trained on 2018 through 2024, without 2020.

The data had 100,669 plate appearances from 265 pitchers. The model used six pitches and seven physical values per pitch.

These scores show separation and classification quality. They do not show that a 30 percent chance occurs 30 percent of the time.

The paper gives no calibration test. SeamScript must add Brier score, log loss, and reliability plots.

## Scope, data, and definitions

Use MLB Statcast pitch data. Group pitches by game and plate appearance. Sort each group by pitch number.

Use 2023 through 2025 for the first model. Train on 2023 and 2024. Test only on 2025.

This window avoids the 2026 ABS change. It also stays within the pitch-timer era. [2023 rules](https://www.mlb.com/rule-changes-2023/) [2026 ABS rules](https://www.mlb.com/press-release/press-release-mlb-announces-abs-challenge-system-coming-to-the-major-leagues-beginning-in-the-2026-season)

Statcast changed from Trackman to Hawk-Eye in 2020. Public bat data begins in April 2024. [Statcast](https://www.mlb.com/glossary/statcast) [Bat tracking](https://www.mlb.com/news/what-you-need-to-know-about-statcast-bat-tracking)

Therefore, do not make bat speed a required model input. Use it only in an optional recent-data study.

Use four evidence labels:

- **Observed rate:** A direct rate in matching records.
- **Estimated chance:** A calibrated model result.
- **Simulated chance:** A result from repeated model paths.
- **Causal effect:** A result from a valid causal design.

The first release must produce the first three labels. It must not produce the fourth label.

## Methodology

### Sequence engine

Parse the seven blocks into an abstract syntax tree. Compile the tree into data, model, and algorithm actions.

A sequence cannot cross a plate-appearance boundary. A missing or changed pitch label must create a warning.

### Comparison engine

Match on pitcher, count, batter side, season, and target pitch type. Add location bands when enough records exist.

Show both sample sizes. Reject a comparison when either group is too small.

Use a plate-appearance bootstrap within pitcher groups. Report the interval and the matched observed difference.

### Probability models

Prefer an approved and calibrated remote model. Use a local baseline only when the catalog approves it.

Build separate probabilities for swing, contact, foul, called strike, and ball-in-play result.

Use the last three pitches. Include type, speed change, movement change, location change, count, and batter side.

Use pitcher history and batter history from prior dates only. This stops future-data leakage.

For an unspecified pitch shape, sample a real matching pitch. Do not combine separate mean values into a false pitch.

### Simulation engine

`method: simulation` starts automatic simulation. The user does not set a seed.

The engine creates a repeatable internal seed from the complete frozen execution plan.

Start with 10,000 trials. Calculate Monte Carlo error for every requested event.

Double the trials when a 95 percent half-width exceeds 0.5 percentage points. Stop at 100,000 trials.

Sample one calibrated bootstrap model for each trial. Then sample the pitch result from that model.

For a full plate appearance, update balls and strikes after each pitch. Stop at a terminal result.

If later pitch choices are not fixed, use the named pitch-choice policy. Label this assumption in the result.

Report sample uncertainty and Monte Carlo error separately. Keep the seed in the protected audit record.

## Remote data, models, and algorithms

A study uses short resource names. A separate catalog maps each name to a local or remote service.

The study contains no address or secret. An administrator owns connection profiles and access rules.

Use Arrow Flight SQL for compatible data systems. Use KServe V2 for compatible prediction services.

Use OpenAPI for other remote algorithms. Use JSON Schema 2020-12 for all input and output contracts.

The compiler checks access, readiness, contracts, and approval state before execution.

A model registry resolves a moving alias to an exact version. A serving endpoint runs that exact version.

The audit record keeps the alias, exact version, digest, data snapshot, and request identifiers.

The runtime controls all calls. A remote algorithm cannot select an undeclared model.

The default failure rule is `on unavailable: stop`. SeamScript never trains an untested replacement model.

[Arrow Flight SQL](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/FlightSql.html) [KServe V2](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/concepts/architecture/data-plane/v2-protocol) [OpenAPI](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html) [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12) [MLflow aliases](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/model-registry/workflow)

## Final language design

Use a stable block grammar with readable values. Do not accept arbitrary English.

The file uses YAML-like keys and indentation. It uses Markdown-like lists and comments. It uses JSON-like strict types.

SeamScript has seven blocks: `study`, `use`, `data`, `sequence`, `compare`, `estimate`, and `show`.

```seam
study: Does a fastball set up a slider?

use:
  data: team pitches
  model:
    outcomes: approved pitch outcome
  algorithm:
    comparison: matched comparison
    simulation: plate appearance simulator
  on unavailable: stop

data:
  seasons: 2023 through 2025
  games: regular season

sequence:
  - fastball
  - slider within 2 pitches

compare:
  against: slider without fastball within 2 pitches before it
  match: pitcher, count, batter side, season
  minimum: 100 sliders per pitcher in each group

estimate:
  event: swing and miss on the slider
  method: simulation
  horizon: this pitch

show:
  - observed rates
  - simulated chance
  - difference
  - uncertainty range
  - strike-zone map
  - 5 example plate appearances
  - calculation details
```

Use two spaces for indentation. Use lower-case names. Reject unknown and duplicate keys.

The study hides the seed and trial controls. `calculation details` shows the trial count and stopping rule.

The hidden seed stays in a protected audit record. Normal output never shows it.

This design is readable once. It is also regular enough to remember and type.

[YAML](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/) [CommonMark](https://spec.commonmark.org/spec) [JSON](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8259/)

## Limits, uncertainty, and checks

Public Statcast shows the delivered pitch. It does not show the catcher’s full intended target.

Observed sequences include selection bias. Pitchers choose pitches for specific counts, batters, and game states.

A model scenario is not a causal result. Never use words such as `caused`, `improved`, or `optimal` for it.

Pitch labels can change across tracking systems and seasons. Record the source label and any mapping.

AUC does not test probability quality. Require calibration by season, pitch type, and sample size.

Test the model on 2025 only after all model choices are final. Also test unseen pitchers as a separate stress test.

Report Brier score, log loss, calibration error, and interval coverage. Report AUC only as a secondary value.

Compare every complex model with a count-and-pitch-type baseline. Keep the simpler model when gains are small.

Full-season impact claims require stronger designs. Defer K/9 and ERA projections.

## Recommended next steps

1. Build the parser for the seven blocks. Add exact errors for unknown keys and values.

2. Build the catalog resolver. Freeze remote aliases to exact versions before execution.

3. Add one data connector, one model connector, and one algorithm connector.

4. Check access, readiness, input contracts, output contracts, approval state, and training cutoff.

5. Prove plate-appearance boundaries and pitch order with one verified Statcast sample.

6. Implement observed rates, matched comparisons, and immediate-pitch simulation.

7. Build one result page. Show results, intervals, samples, examples, and the audit record.

8. Record one demonstration around the fastball-to-slider question.

The first release should answer one question very well. It should not promise a complete pitching adviser.

## Further questions

- Which public Statcast fields remain complete across 2023 through 2025?
- Which minimum sample gives stable pitcher-level comparisons?
- Does a three-pitch history beat a one-pitch history on 2025 calibration?
- Does empirical pitch resampling improve simulation reliability?
- How much does the result change after location matching?
- Can new users write a valid seven-block study without help?
